page.title: React Router Interview Questions and Answers
page.seoTitle: React Router Interview Questions and Answers
page.description: Client side routing, BrowserRouter versus HashRouter, useParams, useNavigate, nested routes, protected routes and data loaders.

intro.text: React has no built-in router, so every real app makes a routing decision, and interviewers use it to check that you understand what a single page app actually does to the browser. The question behind the question is usually: do you know that the URL is state, and that treating it as state solves problems you would otherwise solve badly.

questions.question: What is React Router and why does React need a routing library?
questions.shortAnswer: React renders components; it has no concept of a URL. React Router maps URLs to components and keeps the address bar, history and back button in sync while the page is never actually reloaded.

answer.code:
<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path='/' element={<Home />} />
    <Route path='/products/:id' element={<Product />} />
    <Route path='*' element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

answer.text: It uses the History API to change the URL without a request, then renders the matching route. Frameworks such as Next.js and Remix ship their own routers built on the same idea, usually driven by the file system instead of a component tree.

followUps: Could you write a minimal router yourself?

questions.question: What is the difference between client side routing and server side routing?
questions.shortAnswer: Server routing asks the server for a new HTML document on every navigation. Client routing intercepts the click, changes the URL with the History API and swaps components in place, so no document is fetched.

rows: A full document request and parse
A component swap, and maybe a data fetch
Slower: the bundle must load first
A server rewrite so deep links return the app shell

answer.title: The deployment question hidden in here
answer.text: A client routed app must be served with a catch-all rewrite to `index.html`, or refreshing on `/products/42` returns a 404 because no such file exists. Being able to name this is a strong practical signal.

followUps: Why does refreshing a deep link 404 on a static host?
What does hybrid routing look like in Next.js?

questions.question: What is the difference between BrowserRouter and HashRouter?
questions.shortAnswer: BrowserRouter uses clean URLs through the History API and needs the server to serve the app for every path. HashRouter puts the route after a #, which the server never sees, so it works on any static host with no configuration.

items: `BrowserRouter`: `/products/42`. Clean, crawlable, requires a server rewrite.
`HashRouter`: `/#/products/42`. Works anywhere, but the fragment is never sent to the server, so no server rendering and weaker SEO.
`MemoryRouter` keeps history in memory with no URL at all, which is what you use in tests and in React Native.

answer.text: Use `BrowserRouter` unless you are deploying somewhere you cannot configure, such as a legacy static host or a page embedded in another application.

followUps: Which one would you use inside an Electron app?

questions.question: What is the difference between Link and a plain anchor tag?
questions.shortAnswer: An anchor triggers a full page load, throwing away the app's state and re-downloading everything. Link renders an anchor but intercepts the click and navigates through the router instead.

answer.code: About // full reload About // client navigation About // adds an active state

answer.text: `Link` still renders a real `<a href>`, which matters: middle-click, open in new tab, copy link and crawling all keep working. That is why you should never replace it with a `div` and an `onClick`.

followUps: Why is it important that `Link` renders a real anchor?

questions.question: How do you read route parameters and query strings?
questions.shortAnswer: useParams returns the dynamic segments of the matched path, and useSearchParams gives you a URLSearchParams object plus a setter for the query string.

answer.text: Params are always strings, so convert and validate them. Keeping filters and pagination in the query string rather than in component state is the point worth making: it makes the view shareable, makes the back button correct, and survives a refresh for free.

followUps: Why keep filter state in the URL?

questions.question: How do you navigate programmatically after an action?
questions.shortAnswer: Call the function returned by useNavigate. Pass replace: true when the current entry should not stay in the history, such as after a successful login.

answer.text: Navigating inside an effect that runs on mount is a common way to create a redirect loop. Prefer a `<Navigate>` element in the render, or navigate from the event handler where you know what the user did.

questions.question: What are nested routes, and what does Outlet do?
questions.shortAnswer: Nested routes let a parent route render shared layout and a child route render inside it. Outlet is the placeholder in the parent where React Router renders whichever child matched.

answer.code:
}> } /> } /> function SettingsLayout() { return (
{/* Profile or Billing renders here */}
); }

answer.text: The layout component stays mounted as you move between children, so its state, scroll position and any data it loaded survive the navigation. `index` marks the child shown at the parent's own path.

questions.question: How do you implement a protected route?
questions.shortAnswer: Wrap the routes in a component that checks authentication and either renders an Outlet or redirects to the login page, remembering where the user was trying to go.

items: Handle the loading state explicitly, or the user is bounced to login for a moment while the session is still being checked.
Use `replace` so the protected URL does not sit in the history behind the login page.
Keep the attempted location in `state` so you can send the user back there after signing in.

answer.text: Say this unprompted: a client side guard is a user experience feature, not security. The bundle and the API are both still reachable, so the server must authorise every request regardless.

followUps: How would you handle role based access?

questions.question: How do you code split by route?
questions.shortAnswer: Wrap each route's component in React.lazy with a dynamic import and put a Suspense boundary above the routes, so each route's code downloads only when the user first visits it.

answer.code:
const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./routes/Dashboard'));

<Suspense fallback={<RouteSkeleton />}>
  <Routes>
    <Route path='/dashboard' element={<Dashboard />} />
  </Routes>
</Suspense>

answer.text: React Router's data routers can also declare a `lazy` route, which loads the component and its loader together. Either way, prefetch on hover or on link visibility if the navigation feels slow: the chunk is then usually already in cache by the time the user clicks.

followUps: How would you prefetch a route?

questions.question: What are loaders and actions in React Router's data APIs?
questions.shortAnswer: A loader is a function attached to a route that fetches its data before the route renders; an action handles form submissions to that route. They move data fetching out of components and remove the render-then-fetch waterfall.

items: Data fetching starts as soon as the navigation starts, in parallel with loading the route's code, instead of after the component mounts.
Nested route loaders run in parallel, so a layout and its child do not fetch one after the other.
`errorElement` gives each route its own error boundary, including for loader failures.
This is the same model Remix and the Next.js app router use, which is why it is worth knowing by name.

followUps: How does this compare to fetching in `useEffect`?

questions.question: How do you handle a 404 and redirects?
questions.shortAnswer: Add a catch-all route with path="*" for unmatched URLs, and render <Navigate to="..." replace /> for redirects. Order matters less in modern React Router because it ranks routes by specificity rather than by declaration order.

answer.code:
<Routes>
  <Route path='/' element={<Home />} />
  <Route path='/old-pricing' element={<Navigate to='/pricing' replace />} />
  <Route path='*' element={<NotFound />} />
</Routes>

answer.text: A client side redirect is a 200 response with JavaScript that changes the URL, so search engines do not treat it as a real redirect. For permanent URL changes, issue a 301 from the server or the CDN.

followUps: Why is a client side redirect bad for SEO?
